title: Stochastic Workload Synthesis via Constrained Generative AI: Enhancing Resilience Diagnostics in Containerized Microservices
abstract: Background: Chaos engineering has become the standard method for probing resilience in containerized microservice deployments, but handcrafting workload profiles and fault scenarios does not cover the high-dimensional fault space that production systems inhabit. Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) and stochastic generative modeling offers a path toward automating and diversifying this exploration. Methods: We propose SynthChaos, a constrained generative AI pipeline that combines prompt-engineered LLM fault specification with stochastic variational sampling (TimeVAE) to produce diverse, semantically valid workload profiles. The pipeline was evaluated on a 12-service Kubernetes/Istio/Prometheus testbed across 960 total experiment runs (4 conditions × 4 fault categories × 3 services × 4 workload profiles × 5 replications). All comparisons use Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction; effect sizes are Cliff’s delta. Results: Note: Cliff’s delta computed directly from rank sums (n₁ = n₂ = 5 replications per condition for entropy); U statistics omitted as they are not directly interpretable at this sample size. SynthChaos achieves 23.4% higher coverage entropy than the handcrafted baseline (H = 3.96 vs. 3.21 bits; p < 0.001, δ = 1.00), reduces mean time to detect (MTTD) by 17.2% (29.9 vs. 36.1 s; p < 0.001, δ = 0.68), and improves anomaly detection F1 from 0.785 to 0.836 (p = 0.003, δ = 0.42). Critically, unconstrained LLM generation degrades detection performance (F1: 0.734 vs. 0.785), MTTD (40.6 s vs. 36.1 s), and scenario usability (73.4% vs. 100%) below the handcrafted baseline — while achieving higher raw coverage entropy (3.89 vs. 3.21 bits) at the cost of high variance (SD = 0.31 vs. SD = 0.09 for SynthChaos). RCA top-1 accuracy was 62.5% (SynthChaos) vs. 69.2% (handcrafted), a −6.7 percentage-point difference that was not statistically significant (p = 0.124, Mann-Whitney U), indicating no material RCA degradation at the current sample size. This confirms that structural constraints, not stochastic diversity alone, drive reliable performance gains. Scenario usability reaches 97.6% with only 2.5% generation overhead. Conclusions: Constrained generative AI provides a reproducible and statistically robust foundation for scalable resilience diagnostics. Code, manifests, and raw per-run data are deposited at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21450971).
venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science

title: LLM-assisted generation of intentionally vulnerable containerized environments for cyber ranges
abstract: Cyber ranges are essential training platforms for security teams; however, creating intentionally vulnerable environments remains labor-intensive. While modern virtualization technologies like Docker enable “Infrastructure as Code” approaches, and large language models (LLMs) significantly reduce the effort required for code generation, creating exploitable scenarios remains a challenge. It requires resolving dependencies, configuring interconnected services, and ensuring explicit exploit preconditions, yet the effectiveness of LLMs in realizing these scenarios remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a systematic exploratory study of LLM-assisted generation of intentionally vulnerable containerized environments. We compare different generation paradigms (service-based vs. web applications, package-based vs. source-based builds, and single-container vs. compose-based setups) under zero-shot conditions. We evaluate six LLMs using a two-phase protocol: first, we select the model with the lowest mean Weighted Error Score (WES); second, we conduct an in-depth analysis of paired deployment strategies across 22 vulnerabilities (12 services and 10 web applications), totaling 44 generation attempts and 40 analyzed scenarios (following four ethical refusals). Key findings establish a clear feasibility boundary. While state-of-the-art models (e.g., Gemini3-Pro, GPT-5.2) reduced build failure rates from 81.5% to 51.9%, their ability to generate fully functional, exploitable environments remains limited. Specifically, while functional correctness (build/run) reaches 37.5%–50.0% depending on the strategy, the transition to exploitability represents the primary failure point, with only 5.0% (2/40) of analyzed scenarios proving exploitable. We introduce a repair-oriented analysis based on two metrics to evaluate the change impact and automation challenges of fixing incorrect Dockerfiles. This analysis demonstrates that the choice of strategy significantly affects the repair burden: package-based services require higher structural and automation effort than source-based counterparts, while compose-based web deployments yield better functional outcomes than bundled configurations. Furthermore, our results highlight a practical trade-off in service deployment: despite higher build complexity, source-based reconstruction is preferable for vulnerability fidelity. This is because distribution packages often include downstream security backports that silently mitigate vulnerabilities, even when version identifiers suggest susceptibility. Finally, we provide a taxonomy of build, execution, and exploitation errors. All experimental data, including AI-generated Dockerfiles with annotations and prompts, are publicly available. This study establishes both the potential and the current limitations of zero-shot LLM-based generation, serving as a benchmark for future research into tool-augmented approaches.

title: An Abstention-Aware, Calibrated Risk-Gated Controller for Canary Deployment under Low Observability
abstract: Container deployment automation tools such as Kubernetes-native rollout, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, and Spinnaker/Kayenta gate promotion on operator-defined statistical thresholds do not interpret free-form intent. This paper studies whether coupling a Large Language Model (LLM) and retrieval with a quantitative, confidence-calibrated risk gate improves rollout reliability over such tools. A risk-gated canary controller is defined, in which, at each stage, a normalized composite risk score is computed from health, error-rate, and tail-latency signals and combined with an LLM decision confidence that is calibrated by Platt scaling (logistic calibration of the self-consistency agreement) and evaluated with Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier score. A prototype (Python, Docker, GPT-4o, FAISS retrieval) is evaluated on a Kubernetes cluster under load generated with Locust over n = 20 repetitions against a manual baseline, Kubernetes-native rollout, and an automated canary-analysis baseline; differences are tested with the Mann–Whitney U test. An ablation study isolates the contribution of confidence, retrieval memory, and the risk score, and a weight-sensitivity analysis examines robustness.
venue: Engineering Technology & Applied Science Research

title: Containing the Autonomous Operator: A Defense-in-Depth Framework and Reference Architecture for Securing AI Agents on Kubernetes
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are moving from chat interfaces into infrastructure operations, where they read telemetry, call tools, generate and execute code, and change the state of production Kubernetes clusters. This collapses a boundary that conventional cloud-native security assumes: the boundary between data and control. Content that an agent merely reads (a log line, a ticket, a tool description) can redirect what it does. This paper argues that the model must not be treated as a security boundary and that agent safety on Kubernetes is therefore an infrastructure problem: every guarantee must continue to hold under the assumption that the agent is fully compromised by prompt injection. We contribute (i) a threat model and ten-class threat taxonomy for agents operating on and within Kubernetes, aligned with emerging OWASP guidance for agentic applications; (ii) nine design principles, centered on complete mediation at the tool boundary and on breaking the combination of untrusted input, sensitive access, and external egress; (iii) a seven-layer defense-in-depth framework that maps each principle to native or widely adopted Kubernetes mechanisms: workload identity, RBAC and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, gVisor/Kata sandboxing via the SIG Apps Agent Sandbox project, FQDN-aware egress policy, an agent/MCP gateway with policy-as-code over tool arguments, and eBPF runtime enforcement; (iv) a reference architecture with concrete policy artifacts and per-layer bindings for Amazon EKS, Azure Kubernetes Service, and Google Kubernetes Engine; and (v) a qualitative evaluation comprising a threat-control coverage matrix and four attack walkthroughs, with a proposed empirical methodology. We report no measured attack-success or overhead figures; instead we identify residual risks and the measurements needed to validate the framework.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: Artificial Intelligence and FinTech Innovation in Emerging Markets: The Role of Digital Financial Capabilities and Customer Trust
abstract: This paper investigates the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital Financial Capabilities (DFC) and Customer Trust in digital FinTech Innovation in emerging markets. The statistical research design used was quantitative, cross-sectional, and a questionnaire with five-point Likert scales was used for the collection of data, reaching 300 adult FinTech users. Intelligent automation, predictive analytics, personalized financial services, fraud detection and AI powered decision-support were used to evaluate the impact of AI. The impact of AI was evaluated using the following trends: intelligent automation, predictive analytics, personalized financial services, fraud detection, and AI powered decision-support. DFC identified the skills that the users required to access, understand, assess and safely utilize digital financial technologies and Customer Trust addressed security, reliability, transparency, privacy and responsible service practices. The concept of FinTech Innovation stood for better digital financial products and service delivery, customer experience, personalization and efficiency. Descriptive findings indicated positive perceptions on all constructs ranging from mean scores of 3.92 (SD = 0.71) for AI to 3.79 (SD = 0.76) for Customer Trust and 3.95 (SD = 0.69) for FinTech Innovation for DFC. The reliability tests showed low item-total correlation, with the overall .24 item-total alpha range from .89 (AI) to .92 (FinTech Innovation), and .91 (Customer Trust), .87 (DFC), and .89 (AI). The results highlighted that the capital markets in emerging markets need technological intelligence, users who can apply the technology and trustworthy digital environments. It is crucial to address issues of customer-friendly technology governance, customer security, privacy safeguarding, transparency, and transformational digital financial education in the governance of inclusive and sustainable innovations in the financial sector with the help of artificial intelligence technologies, the study has pointed out. title: Development of RAG-Based Generative AI Application: Application of Generative AI in RAG-Based Web Development
abstract: Abstract The rapid evolution of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) has transformed the landscape of intelligent web application development. Despite their remarkable fluency, standalone LLMs frequently suffer from hallucination, outdated knowledge, and an inability to reference verifiable, domain-specific information, which limits their reliability in enterprise contexts. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by coupling a parametric language model with a non-parametric retrieval mechanism that fetches relevant information from an external knowledge base at inference time. This paper presents the design, methodology, and prototype architecture of a RAG-based generative AI web application intended to demonstrate how retrieval, semantic search, and prompt engineering can be combined with modern web development practices to build context-aware, factually grounded AI systems. The proposed system integrates a document ingestion and chunking pipeline, sentence-level embedding generation, a vector database for high-dimensional semantic search, and a large language model layer responsible for grounded response generation. The web application is designed using a React.js/Next.js frontend, a FastAPI/Node.js backend, JWT-based authentication, and a cloud-native deployment strategy using Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD pipelines on platforms such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform. The paper reviews recent literature on RAG architectures, compares leading vector databases (Pinecone, FAISS, ChromaDB, Milvus) and embedding models, and surveys contributions from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta AI, Microsoft Research, Hugging Face, LangChain, and LlamaIndex. Rather than reporting fabricated experimental numbers, this work proposes a rigorous evaluation methodology — covering retrieval accuracy, groundedness, latency, and user satisfaction — that can be applied once the prototype is fully deployed. The study concludes that RAG-based architectures offer a practical, scalable, and enterprise-ready pathway toward building trustworthy generative AI web applications, while identifying open challenges such as embedding quality, context-window constraints, and operational cost that motivate future work in agentic and multimodal RAG systems. Keywords: Generative AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Large Language Models (LLMs), Prompt Engineering, Vector Database, Semantic Search, AI Chatbot, Web Development, Cloud Deployment, Enterprise Applications.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: LLM-Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning for Distributed Cloud Resource Scheduling
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for automating cloud resource scheduling, yet conventional RL-based schedulers often lack interpretability, violate service-level objectives (SLOs), and introduce substantial deployment risks in Kubernetes environments. In this paper, we propose a hybrid framework that integrates large language models (LLMs), safe reinforcement learning, and a digital twin simulator for distributed cloud resource scheduling. Rather than using the LLM as a direct decision-maker, our approach leverages it to generate scheduling constraints from SLO documents and historical cluster events, adjust reward functions, and produce human-readable explanations. A Proximal Policy Optimization agent with Lagrangian relaxation (PPO-Lagrangian) executes scheduling actions—including pod placement, autoscaling, and resource quota allocation—subject to the LLM-derived constraints. Before deployment, candidate policies are pre-evaluated in a digital twin simulator synchronized with the target cluster, and only policies passing safety verification are applied. We evaluate the framework on Google Online Boutique deployed on a Kubernetes cluster simulator under periodic, burst, and fault-injection workloads. Compared with five baselines, our approach reduces SLO violation rates by 39–68% and lowers normalized resource costs by 14–34% while maintaining competitive response times. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component to overall performance.
venue: Preprints.org

title: From Security Findings to Verified Fixes: Automated Repair of Infrastructure-as-Code Misconfigurations
abstract: Traditional Infrastructure as Code misconfiguration remediation requires manual analysis, a labor-intensive approach that cannot meet the scale and speed demands of modern cloud deployments. We present IacFix, an agentic tool that combines LLM-based agents with formal methods to enable automated IaC security remediation from security findings to validated patches. IacFix introduces end-to-end remediation capabilities across CDK and CloudFormation packages, leveraging historical fix patterns and iterative refinement to produce validated patches for complex misconfigurations. For example, IacFix achieves 80.9% end-to-end success rate with 97.7% fault localization precision and 7.12 minutes average processing time, demonstrating comparable effectiveness to manual fixes while delivering automated solutions significantly faster. Notably, IacFix outperforms LLM-only baselines by 45 percentage points in real-world scenarios such as dangling hostclass remediation. The system exhibits one-sided error: it either produces a validated patch or safely declines to patch, ensuring that no incorrect patch is surfaced to developers. Our approach shows promising potential for addressing diverse misconfiguration types at scale.
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: CTForge: Automatically Generating Test Suites for Software Configuration
abstract: Software configuration plays a critical role in modern software systems, yet it also frequently leads to severe failures. Existing approaches, whether static analysis or LLM-based validation, struggle to capture implicit semantic constraints and validate configuration-code interactions. Leveraging existing unit tests is also insufficient due to their lack of configuration-specific focus. Thus, we present CTForge, an LLM-powered framework that automatically generates configuration-specific test suites. Its core innovation is a three-stage configuration-aware optimization pipeline that moves beyond vanilla test generation, specifically using parameter semantics to improve LLM outputs. This optimization pipeline iteratively aligns tests through: (1)enhance configuration-related code coverage to ensure relevance, (2) assertion validation across valid parameter values to eliminate false assertions, and (3) configuration-sensitivity verification to select tests that semantically exercise the intended configuration behavior. Evaluated on five large-scale systems, CTForge detects 63 out of 79 real-world configuration issues and achieves an F1-score of 0.88 in misconfiguration detection. CTForge also uncovers six previously unknown defects. Our work demonstrates that structured configuration-aware refinement is essential for LLM to produce effective test suites.
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: Exact-IaC: Execution-Driven Exact Knowledge Injection for Reliable IaC Synthesis
abstract: The deployment and maintenance of software systems rely heavily on Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) to translate high-level infrastructure intent into deployable configurations. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show potential in automating IaC synthesis, relying on closed-source cloud APIs poses severe data privacy risks. Conversely, deploying Small Language Models (SLMs) locally often encounters performance bottlenecks due to schema hallucinations and attention dilution in long-context scenarios. Furthermore, existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-turn repair, and semantic topology parsing approaches struggle to resolve complex declarative resource dependencies.
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: Towards Reliable Agentic Infrastructure Provisioning with LLMs
abstract: Kubernetes (K8s) is widely used to orchestrate containerized workloads, yet provisioning reliable and maintainable clusters requires substantial DevOps and cloud-infrastructure expertise. This paper presents an LLM-based Infrastructure-as-Code workflow for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) that combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with a bounded validation-and-repair loop. The workflow retrieves contextual examples from a curated Terraform knowledge base, generates infrastructure configurations, validates them, and returns recoverable errors to the model for correction. We evaluate the approach through two complementary studies. First, an exploratory infrastructure-provisioning benchmark assesses six commercial LLMs across five prompt variants using the complete retrieval-and-repair workflow to provision AWS EKS infrastructure. Second, a controlled 2 × 2 ablation independently enables and disables retrieval and iterative repair for three representative models. This ablation includes five prompt variants and three repetitions per model-condition combination, totaling 180 plan-only executions. Under the complete workflow, Terraform plan success reached 100% for Claude Opus 4.5, 93.3% for GPT-4.1, and 100% for Gemini 3.1 Pro, compared with one-shot baseline rates of 86.7%, 0%, and 46.7%, respectively. The results show that retrieval and repair have model-dependent effects, while their combination achieved the highest or joint-highest plan success for all reevaluated models.

title: Energy-Aware Agentic Orchestration for Multi-Site Service Deployment
abstract: Energy-aware orchestration across geographically distributed infrastructures is increasingly important as data centers absorb growing Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads. However, existing approaches often exclude the energy cost of automated decision-making from system-level sustainability assessments. This paper presents an energy-aware agentic orchestration framework that treats Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning as a measurable component of the control loop. We compare single-shot tool calling, ReAct, and plan-and-execute strategies on a multi-site Kubernetes testbed spanning two European data centers and instrumented at layers ranging from power distribution units to per-pod energy attribution. Using ten natural-language orchestration intents with varying decision complexity, we show that reasoning strategy and intent complexity strongly influence graphics processing unit (GPU) energy consumption during orchestration decisions. ReAct and plan-and-execute generated executable tool calls across all evaluated intents but required multiple LLM inferences, whereas the single-shot configuration was less costly but non-actionable. Prefix caching reduced mean ReAct GPU energy consumption by 29.4%. For the evaluated lightweight workload, the infrastructure-energy changes observed within the one-second measurement window were insufficient to offset the measured GPU decision energy. These findings demonstrate the importance of accounting for reasoning overhead when assessing the sustainability of AI-native orchestration and motivate energy-budgeted selection of agent strategies.
venue: arXiv (Cornell University)

title: DriftAgent: Using a Language Model to Turn Terraform Drift into Reviewed Merge Requests
abstract: Purpose: This paper describes the design and operation of DriftAgent, a system that detects configuration drift in Terraform-managed cloud infrastructure and prepares fixes for human review. It also reports what we learned from running the system in production at a streaming television company. Methodology: The study used a single-site case study design to evaluate a production deployment. DriftAgent runs every weekday morning: it asks an Atlantis server to plan 187 Terraform projects in parallel, parses the plan output, and sends each drifted project, together with its source files, to a large language model in a single request. The model returns HCL changes, including Terraform import blocks for resources that exist in the cloud but not in state; the agent opens a GitLab merge request for human review and posts a daily summary to Slack. Over twelve weeks (56 runs), we measured four outcomes: the fate of each merge request (merged unchanged, merged after edits, or closed), plan sweep time, engineering time per drift event, and inference cost. Merge request outcomes were validated by two engineers who independently rated a random sample of 120 merge requests as acceptable, acceptable with edits, or unacceptable against defined criteria, and inter-rater reliability was measured with Cohen’s kappa. Engineering effort was compared with a pre-deployment timing study of 71 manually handled drift events. Data were analyzed with descriptive statistics (counts, percentages, means, medians, and 95th percentiles), edited or closed proposals were classified by their main failure reason, and the findings were synthesized by triangulating production logs, merge request histories, the independent ratings, and the timing data. Findings: Across 56 runs the system recorded 372 drift events and opened 351 merge requests. Reviewers merged 73.5% of them without semantic changes and 18.2% after edits, and closed 8.3%. Moving plan execution from a sequential loop to Atlantis reduced the median sweep time from 52.0 to 11.4 minutes. Weekly engineering time spent on drift fell from 9.4 to 2.4 hours, at an inference cost of about US$0.08 per drifted project. The most common reasons for edited or rejected proposals were choosing the wrong kind of remediation and formatting an import identifier incorrectly. Unique contribution to theory, practice and policy: The study gives evidence that a fixed workflow with one model call, a deterministic plan check, and mandatory human approval is a workable way to use language models in change-controlled infrastructure. For practitioners, it documents specific design choices and failure modes. For organizations writing policy on AI in operations, it supports keeping approval and apply rights with people while assigning analysis and drafting to the model.
venue: International Journal of Computing and Engineering

title: Scaffolder or Agent? Measuring the Organizational-Conformance Cost of Replacing Golden-Path Generators with LLM Agents
abstract: Replication package for the ICSE-SEIP 2027 paper "Scaffolder or Agent? Measuring the Organizational-Conformance Cost of Replacing Golden-Path Generators with LLM Agents". It contains the deterministic golden-path scaffolder, the convention-layer evaluators (Python and OPA/Conftest), the task corpus, all generated Terraform configurations with per-cell metric CSVs, and the analysis scripts. Every number in the paper can be re-derived without re-running any model or using cloud credentials. Start with ARTIFACT.md. Code is MIT; data is CC BY 4.0.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Operationalizing OWASP LLM Top 10 Controls in Enterprise AI Platforms
abstract: Enterprises have moved large language model applications from pilot projects into production systems handling customer conversations, internal knowledge retrieval, and increasingly autonomous agentic workflows, introducing a risk surface that differs materially from what conventional application security programs address. OWASP has responded with the Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, most recently revised in its 2025 edition, and a newly published Top 10 for Agentic Applications covering autonomous, tool-using systems. These taxonomies name and prioritize risk but leave engineering teams to translate categories such as prompt injection or excessive agency into controls that fit an existing cloud-native delivery pipeline. This paper proposes a reference architecture and implementation framework mapping each of the ten OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 categories to specific, deployable controls built on commonly used cloud primitives: managed model gateways, service mesh identity, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and continuous delivery tooling. The framework is informed by production engineering practice with retrieval-augmented generation and agentic workloads on Kubernetes using a managed foundation model service. Five real, publicly documented incidents, including a corporate data leak, a manipulated dealership chatbot, a legal ruling on chatbot liability, an indirect prompt injection exfiltration attack, and a zero-click vulnerability in a widely used enterprise copilot, are analyzed against the proposed controls to show where the framework would have reduced impact or prevented the incident outright. A four-stage maturity model helps organizations sequence adoption. Open challenges discussed include the immaturity of evaluation tooling for non-deterministic systems and the persistent tension between guardrail thoroughness and production latency.
venue: Journal of Technology and Systems
